PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
Amends the California Constitution to remove the choice of a successor from recall elections.
Allows vacancies created by recalls to be filled under succession rules for state officers.
...
Proposition 5 would amend the California Constitution to change how state officer recall elections work in three key ways.^1^
First, when voters choose to recall an elected official, they also choose that person’s successor on the same ballot.
Prop.
5 would eliminate the successor election and instead fill the office through existing constitutional succession rules.
These rules require the governor to fill non-legislative office vacancies (e.g., secretary of state, attorney general, controller) by appointment, and special elections to fill legislative office vacancies (senator, assemblymember).
Second, if a governor is recalled, Prop.
5 would require the lieutenant governor to assume the governorship for the remainder of the term.
If the governor is successfully recalled before the close of nomination for the next statewide election, a special election would be held at the next statewide primary.
This special election would prevent an unelected appointed governor from holding office for a full four-year term.^2^
Third, Prop.
5 removes the prohibition on recalled officers running for the same office in a subsequent special election to fill their seat.

Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them.
This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election.
The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election.
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected.

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.
Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office.
In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.
The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
***Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor.*** The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs.
If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election.
If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.

The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.

How this is built
Proposition 5 is forecast as a elections measure whose Yes vote leans Democratic . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes.
Prop 5 would eliminate that second section.
If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.

The picture is clear:

- Both polls show the measure trailing: PPIC 45-52 (Oct), IGS/LAT 37-57 (Oct 19-25).
- Trend improving for yes (35→45 in PPIC) but still behind.
- Almost no money on either side; Yes committee ~$28K + in-kind; opposition from CA GOP, Reform California, Election Integrity Project.
- Author "not optimistic."
- Forecast: 45.7% chance to pass, 54.3% no.
- Newspapers largely against (Bay Area News Group: No; check others).

Also relevant: low-salience measures with weak name recognition generally don't get a late surge in a midterm with 14 props. And the "no" argument ("politicians would choose") is a powerful, simple message.

One counterpoint: in midterms, Democratic-leaning turnout is higher, and 56% of Democrats support it. But 44% of Democrats oppose and 40% of independents. Overall polling average is 43% yes. Base rates: measures polling below 45% two weeks out rarely pass.

Let me quickly check the endorsement table for a broader picture and any final polls. Actually, the evidence is sufficient. But let me do one more check on the IGS endorsements table and possibly the latest news from Nov 2-3 to see if anything changed.

For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.

Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.

The picture is clear:

- Both polls show the measure trailing: PPIC 45-52 (Oct), IGS/LAT 37-57 (Oct 19-25).
- Trend improving for yes (35→45 in PPIC) but still behind.
- Almost no money on either side; Yes committee ~$28K + in-kind; opposition from CA GOP, Reform California, Election Integrity Project.
- Author "not optimistic."
- Forecast: 45.7% chance to pass, 54.3% no.
- Newspapers largely against (Bay Area News Group: No; check others).

Also relevant: low-salience measures with weak name recognition generally don't get a late surge in a midterm with 14 props. And the "no" argument ("politicians would choose") is a powerful, simple message.

One counterpoint: in midterms, Democratic-leaning turnout is higher, and 56% of Democrats support it. But 44% of Democrats oppose and 40% of independents. Overall polling average is 43% yes. Base rates: measures polling below 45% two weeks out rarely pass.

Let me quickly check the endorsement table for a broader picture and any final polls. Actually, the evidence is sufficient. But let me do one more check on the IGS endorsements table and possibly the latest news from Nov 2-3 to see if anything changed.

# Proposition 5
Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Recall of State Officials.*** The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall.
A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office.
To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices).
...
***Two Questions in Recall Elections.*** In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office.
The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies.
For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election.
If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
...
The process to fill a vacant office varies by office.
Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor.
The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor.
Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal

#### Proposition 5
##### Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy.
Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

# Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
## Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
...
### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Removes Second Question From Recall Elections.*** Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election.
This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
***Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices.*** If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant.
Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office.
In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.
The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
***Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor.*** The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs.
If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election.
If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.

### Additional Titles

### Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023.
As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters.
The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024.
The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process.
Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled.
If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law.
Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor.
If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.

The picture is clear:

- Both polls show the measure trailing: PPIC 45-52 (Oct), IGS/LAT 37-57 (Oct 19-25).
- Trend improving for yes (35→45 in PPIC) but still behind.
- Almost no money on either side; Yes committee ~$28K + in-kind; opposition from CA GOP, Reform California, Election Integrity Project.
- Author "not optimistic."
- Forecast: 45.7% chance to pass, 54.3% no.
- Newspapers largely against (Bay Area News Group: No; check others).

Also relevant: low-salience measures with weak name recognition generally don't get a late surge in a midterm with 14 props. And the "no" argument ("politicians would choose") is a powerful, simple message.

One counterpoint: in midterms, Democratic-leaning turnout is higher, and 56% of Democrats support it. But 44% of Democrats oppose and 40% of independents. Overall polling average is 43% yes. Base rates: measures polling below 45% two weeks out rarely pass.

Let me quickly check the endorsement table for a broader picture and any final polls. Actually, the evidence is sufficient. But let me do one more check on the IGS endorsements table and possibly the latest news from Nov 2-3 to see if anything changed.
